blocks.body:
Is $7382916$ divisible by $9$? What are the last two digits of $7^{2026}$? How many numbers in row $100$ of Pascal's triangle are odd? Each question is phrased in terms of how a number is written, but each is really a question about arithmetic. The bridge is one observation: writing $n$ in base $b$ means writing $n$ as a polynomial evaluated at $b$, and congruences let us replace $b$ by something simpler, such as $1$ or $-1$.

This lesson sets up base representations carefully, derives the tests for $9$ and $11$, explains what the last few digits of a number record, and ends with a less obvious fact: the carries you make when adding two numbers in base $2$ count the factors of $2$ in a binomial coefficient.

blocks.title: Writing a number in base b
blocks.body:
Our usual notation is shorthand: $2026$ means $2\cdot 10^3 + 0\cdot 10^2 + 2\cdot 10 + 6$. Nothing is special about ten. In base $2$ we have $13 = 8 + 4 + 1 = (1101)_2$, and you can find these digits by repeated division by $2$:

$$13 = 2\cdot 6 + 1,\qquad 6 = 2\cdot 3 + 0,\qquad 3 = 2\cdot 1 + 1,\qquad 1 = 2\cdot 0 + 1.$$

Reading the remainders from the last line up gives $1101$. The first remainder is the last digit, because $13 \equiv 1 \pmod 2$; dividing out removes that digit and shifts the rest one place to the right.

blocks.title: Base-b representation
blocks.body:
Fix an integer $b \ge 2$. A base-$b$ representation of a positive integer $n$ is an expression

$$n = \sum_{i=0}^{k} a_i b^i = a_k b^k + a_{k-1}b^{k-1} + \dots + a_1 b + a_0$$

with integers $0 \le a_i < b$ and $a_k \ne 0$. We write $n = (a_k a_{k-1}\dots a_0)_b$, call the $a_i$ the digits, and write $s_b(n) = a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_k$ for the base-$b$ digit sum.

In words: the digits are the successive remainders when you keep dividing by $b$.

blocks.title: Existence and uniqueness of digits
blocks.body: Let $b \ge 2$. Every positive integer has exactly one base-$b$ representation.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
We use strong induction on $n$. Divide: $n = bq + r$ with $0 \le r < b$.

If $n < b$, then $n = a_0$ with $a_0 = n$ is a representation. It is the only one, since a representation with $k \ge 1$ has value at least $a_k b^k \ge b > n$.

If $n \ge b$, then $1 \le q < n$. By induction $q = \sum_{i=0}^{j} c_i b^i$ for some digits $c_i$, and then $n = \sum_{i=0}^{j} c_i b^{i+1} + r$ is a base-$b$ representation of $n$. For uniqueness, take any representation $n = \sum_{i=0}^k a_i b^i$. Here $k \ge 1$ because $n \ge b$, and

$$n = b\,(a_1 + a_2 b + \dots + a_k b^{k-1}) + a_0,\qquad 0 \le a_0 < b.$$

Quotient and remainder in the division algorithm are unique, so $a_0 = r$ and $a_1 + a_2 b + \dots + a_k b^{k-1} = q$. The right-hand side is a base-$b$ representation of $q$, which is unique by the induction hypothesis. So all the $a_i$ are determined by $n$.

blocks.title: How many digits, and what the last ones mean
blocks.body:
Two quick consequences. First, $n$ has $k+1$ digits exactly when $b^k \le n < b^{k+1}$, that is, the number of base-$b$ digits is $\lfloor \log_b n \rfloor + 1$. For instance $2^{2026}$ has $\lfloor 2026\log_{10} 2\rfloor + 1 = 610$ decimal digits.

Second, the last $m$ digits of $n$ are exactly the remainder of $n$ modulo $b^m$, because

$$n = (a_{m-1}\dots a_1 a_0)_b + b^m\,(a_m + a_{m+1}b + \dots).$$

So "find the last two digits" means "compute modulo $100$", and $n$ is divisible by $b^m$ exactly when its last $m$ digits are zero. In base $10$, divisibility by $2^m$ or $5^m$ depends only on the last $m$ digits, since both divide $10^m$. Computing modulo $100$ is a job for [[fermat-euler]] and, by splitting $100 = 4\cdot 25$, for [[crt]].

blocks.title: Digit sums: working modulo b - 1 and b + 1
blocks.body:
Here is the main idea. Put $P(x) = a_k x^k + \dots + a_1 x + a_0$, a polynomial with integer coefficients, so that $n = P(b)$. If $b \equiv c \pmod m$ then $P(b) \equiv P(c) \pmod m$, because congruences respect sums and products ([[congruences]]). Two choices of $m$ make $c$ very simple:

1. $m = b - 1$: then $b \equiv 1$, and $P(1) = a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_k$ is the digit sum.
2. $m = b + 1$: then $b \equiv -1$, and $P(-1) = a_0 - a_1 + a_2 - \dots$ is the alternating digit sum, starting with a plus sign at the units digit.

In base $10$ this gives the familiar tests: $n$ and its digit sum leave the same remainder modulo $9$ (hence also modulo $3$), and $n$ and its alternating digit sum leave the same remainder modulo $11$. For $n = 7382916$ the digit sum is $36$, so $9 \mid n$; the alternating sum is $6 - 1 + 9 - 2 + 8 - 3 + 7 = 24$, so $n \equiv 24 \equiv 2 \pmod{11}$.

blocks.title: Digit-sum congruences
blocks.body:
Let $n = \sum_{i=0}^{k} a_i b^i$ be the base-$b$ representation of $n$. Then

$$n \equiv s_b(n) \pmod{b-1},\qquad n \equiv \sum_{i=0}^{k} (-1)^i a_i \pmod{b+1}.$$

In particular $n \equiv s_{10}(n) \pmod 9$.

Since $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$, every power satisfies $b^i \equiv 1$, so $\sum a_i b^i \equiv \sum a_i$. Since $b \equiv -1 \pmod{b+1}$, we get $b^i \equiv (-1)^i$, so $\sum a_i b^i \equiv \sum (-1)^i a_i$.

blocks.title: Carries and the digit sum
blocks.body:
Digit sums are not additive: $s_{10}(5) + s_{10}(7) = 12$ but $s_{10}(12) = 3$. The discrepancy is caused by carries, and it is easy to measure. When you add two numbers in base $b$ column by column, a carry happens when a column total $t$ is at least $b$: you write $t - b$ and pass $1$ to the next column. The digits of the answer lose $b$ in one column and gain $1$ in the next, a net loss of $b - 1$.

To make this exact, let $m$ and $n$ have digits $x_i$ and $y_i$, and let $\varepsilon_i \in \{0,1\}$ be the carry out of column $i$, with $\varepsilon_{-1} = 0$. (A carry is at most $1$, since a column total is at most $(b-1)+(b-1)+1 = 2b-1$.) The digit of $m+n$ in column $i$ is $z_i = x_i + y_i + \varepsilon_{i-1} - b\,\varepsilon_i$. Summing over all columns, including the one that receives the final carry, and writing $C$ for the number of carries:

$$s_b(m+n) = s_b(m) + s_b(n) + C - bC,\qquad\text{so}\qquad s_b(m) + s_b(n) - s_b(m+n) = (b-1)\,C.$$

In base $2$, where $b - 1 = 1$, the loss in digit sum is exactly the number of carries. That is the link to binomial coefficients.

blocks.title: Carries count factors of 2
blocks.body:
For integers $m, n \ge 0$,

$$\nu_2\!\binom{m+n}{m} = \#\{\text{carries when adding } m,n \text{ in base } 2\}.$$

First we compute $\nu_2(N!)$, the exponent of $2$ in $N!$. An integer $j \le N$ with $\nu_2(j) = e$ is a multiple of $2, 4, \dots, 2^e$ and of no higher power of $2$, so it is counted exactly $e$ times in the sum $\sum_{k\ge1} \#\{j \le N : 2^k \mid j\}$. Hence $\nu_2(N!) = \sum_{k \ge 1}\lfloor N/2^k\rfloor$. (This is Legendre's formula, treated for all primes in [[binomial-factorial]].)

Now write $N = \sum_i a_i 2^i$ in binary. Dividing by $2^k$ and discarding the fractional part removes the last $k$ digits, so $\lfloor N/2^k\rfloor = \sum_{i \ge k} a_i 2^{i-k}$. Summing over $k \ge 1$, the digit $a_i$ is counted with weight $2^{i-1} + \dots + 2 + 1 = 2^i - 1$, so

$$\nu_2(N!) = \sum_i a_i(2^i - 1) = N - s_2(N).$$

Finally

$$\nu_2\!\binom{m+n}{m} = \nu_2((m+n)!) - \nu_2(m!) - \nu_2(n!) = s_2(m) + s_2(n) - s_2(m+n),$$

which is the number of carries by the identity above with $b = 2$.

blocks.title: Even palindromes
blocks.body: Prove that every palindrome with an even number of decimal digits is divisible by $11$. Does the same hold for palindromes with an odd number of digits?
blocks.solution:
Let the digits be $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{2k-1}$ (from the units digit up), with $a_i = a_{2k-1-i}$ for every $i$. By the digit-sum congruences, $n \equiv \sum_i (-1)^i a_i \pmod{11}$.

Pair index $i$ with index $2k-1-i$. Their sum $2k-1$ is odd, so one index is even and the other is odd: the two equal digits $a_i = a_{2k-1-i}$ enter the alternating sum with opposite signs and cancel. Every index is in exactly one pair, so the alternating sum is $0$ and $11 \mid n$. For example $123321 = 11 \cdot 11211$.

For an odd number of digits the middle digit has no partner, and the claim fails: $121 = 11^2$ is divisible by $11$, but $101$ is not.

blocks.title: Last two digits
blocks.body: Find the last two digits of $7^{2026}$ and of $2^{2026}$.
blocks.solution:
We work modulo $100$. For $7$ there is a shortcut: $7^2 = 49$ and $7^4 = 2401 \equiv 1 \pmod{100}$. Since $2026 = 4\cdot 506 + 2$,

$$7^{2026} = (7^4)^{506}\cdot 7^2 \equiv 49 \pmod{100}.$$

For $2$ we cannot use Euler's theorem modulo $100$ directly, since $\gcd(2,100) \ne 1$, so we split $100 = 4 \cdot 25$. Modulo $4$, $2^{2026} \equiv 0$. Modulo $25$, Euler's theorem gives $2^{20} \equiv 1$, and $2026 = 20\cdot 101 + 6$, so $2^{2026} \equiv 2^6 = 64 \equiv 14 \pmod{25}$. The numbers below $100$ that are $\equiv 14 \pmod{25}$ are $14, 39, 64, 89$, and the only multiple of $4$ among them is $64$.

So $7^{2026}$ ends in $49$ and $2^{2026}$ ends in $64$.

blocks.title: A digit sum of a digit sum of a digit sum
blocks.solution:
The idea is that $C$ is congruent to $2^{2026}$ modulo $9$, and repeated digit sums shrink numbers so fast that $C$ must be small. We bound first, then reduce.

Bounds. As computed above, $2^{2026}$ has $610$ digits, each at most $9$, so $A \le 9\cdot 610 = 5490$. A number at most $5490$ has digit sum at most $31$: if its thousands digit is $5$, its hundreds digit is at most $4$ and the digit sum is at most $5+4+9+9 = 27$; otherwise the digit sum is at most $4+9+9+9 = 31$. So $B \le 31$. A number at most $31$ has digit sum at most $11$ (attained at $29$). So $1 \le C \le 11$.

Congruence. Taking digit sums preserves the remainder modulo $9$, so $C \equiv 2^{2026} \pmod 9$. Since $2^6 = 64 \equiv 1 \pmod 9$ and $2026 = 6\cdot 337 + 4$, we get $2^{2026} \equiv 2^4 = 16 \equiv 7 \pmod 9$.

The only integer in $[1, 11]$ that is $\equiv 7 \pmod 9$ is $7$. Hence $C = 7$.

blocks.title: Odd entries of Pascal's triangle
blocks.body: Show that the number of odd entries in row $N$ of Pascal's triangle, that is, the number of $m \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}$ with $\binom{N}{m}$ odd, equals $2^{s_2(N)}$. How many odd entries does row $100$ have, and which are they?
blocks.solution:
By the theorem on carries, $\binom{N}{m}$ is odd exactly when adding $m$ and $N - m$ in binary produces no carries.

Claim: there are no carries exactly when every binary digit $1$ of $m$ sits in a position where $N$ also has a $1$. If there are no carries, each binary digit of $N$ is the plain sum of the corresponding digits of $m$ and $N-m$; a digit of $N$ is at most $1$, so wherever $m$ has a $1$, $N$ has a $1$ (and $N-m$ has a $0$). Conversely, if the $1$s of $m$ are among the $1$s of $N$, then $N - m$ is the number whose binary $1$s are the remaining positions of $N$, and adding $m$ and $N - m$ never puts two $1$s in one column, so there are no carries.

So the valid $m$ correspond to subsets of the set of positions where $N$ has a $1$. There are $s_2(N)$ such positions and hence $2^{s_2(N)}$ subsets.

For $N = 100 = (1100100)_2 = 64 + 32 + 4$ we have $s_2(100) = 3$, so row $100$ has $2^3 = 8$ odd entries: those with $m$ a sum of a subset of $\{4, 32, 64\}$, namely $m = 0, 4, 32, 36, 64, 68, 96, 100$.

blocks.body:
- The digit-sum test works modulo $9$ and its divisors only, not modulo $27$: $1899$ has digit sum $27$, but $1899 = 27\cdot 70 + 9$ is not divisible by $27$. In base $b$ the digit sum controls only divisors of $b - 1$.
- The alternating sum for $11$ starts with a plus sign at the units digit. Starting from the leading digit changes the sign when the number of digits is even; that is harmless for testing divisibility but gives the wrong remainder.
- Uniqueness of digits needs $0 \le a_i < b$. Allow a digit equal to $b$ and $10 = (10)_{10}$ could also be written as a single digit "ten".
- Digit sums satisfy $s_b(m+n) \le s_b(m) + s_b(n)$, with equality exactly when there are no carries. When counting carries, include the one out of the top column: adding $1 + 1$ in base $2$ makes one carry, matching $\nu_2\binom{2}{1} = 1$.

The carry theorem works for every prime $p$, not just $2$: the exponent of $p$ in $\binom{m+n}{m}$ is the number of carries in base $p$ (Kummer's theorem), and $\nu_p(N!) = (N - s_p(N))/(p-1)$. Both are in [[binomial-factorial]], built on [[p-adic-valuation]]. The digit-by-digit description of $\binom{N}{m}$ modulo $p$ is [[lucas]]. The digit count $\lfloor \log_b n\rfloor + 1$ is a typical use of [[floor-functions]], and expansions of real numbers in base $b$ have a cousin in [[continued-fractions]].

In computer science, base $2$ is how machines do arithmetic. Carries decide the cost of addition circuits, digit sums of binary numbers (population counts) appear throughout algorithm design, and the binary splitting of indices is what organises the Fast Fourier Transform.

1. Write $2026$ in base $2$ and in base $7$.
2. Show that a number written in base $7$ is divisible by $6$ exactly when its digit sum is, and by $8$ exactly when its alternating digit sum is.
3. Find the remainder of $918082$ modulo $11$ and modulo $9$ without dividing. Then find the smallest positive integer whose decimal digit sum is $2026$.
4. For which $N$ are all of $\binom{N}{0}, \binom{N}{1}, \dots, \binom{N}{N}$ odd?
